new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (Gordon; antepenultimate stress = antepenultimate, initial in 1-3-syllable words) rests on Collier & Collier 1975 for the Apoze dialect. Johnson describes the Kuwi/Kui dialect of the same language and gives penultimate stress, a different placement. The two are different dialects (the OPD sheets say each of the six Kela villages is a different dialect), so this is a dialect split rather than a refutation of the Apoze statement; it does mean a language-level 'antepenult' coding does not hold for all of kcl, and it points the same way as the penult-default description in Ransdell-Green 2022 that the webcat check for kela1255 already recommends as the deciding source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Kuwi (Kui) dialect stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable. (The sheet's spelling 'penulimately' is the original's.) The bold syllables in the following 'Syllable Patterns' table mark the syllable type being exemplified, not stress, so they carry no counter-evidence.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; nothing on tone or length beyond the section heading
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are dialect-specific. Collier & Collier 1975 describe the Apoze dialect (village Lokanu', about 200 speakers; 'a little further removed from the Kela norm than any of the other villages', p. 129); the catalog record (Gordon; WALS 'Kela (Apoze)') is this variety. Johnson 1994 describes the Kuwi dialect (the task list calls it Kui; the village list on the sheet includes Kui). The OPD sheets state that each of the six Kela villages (Keila, Lagui/Lagwi, Laukanu/Lokanu, Lababia, Buso, Kui) is a different dialect.

new_statements.quote: Tone was not recorded in Apoze dialect. Stress is not emic, as a consistent pattern was found to explain its occurrence. In one, two, and three syllable words, the stress is on the first syllable. One exception was found: /awe/ [a'we] 'yesterday' /awe/ ['awe] 'lizard' Where the word has more than three syllables, the stress is on the third last syllable. [p. 150:] There are predictable exceptions to this rule. Where a word has a qualifying affix, the stress remains on the main (qualified) word. /aŋazi/ [aŋ'azi] 'his father' /azi/ ['azi] 'father' /moaliliŋa/ ['moaliliŋa] 'death adder' /moa/ ['moa] 'snake' No variation in length of vocoids or contoids was recorded, apart from syllabic n [n̩].
new_statements.citation: Collier, Margaret and Collier, Kenneth J. (1975). A tentative phonemic statement of the Apoze dialect, Kela language. In Phonologies of five Austronesian languages. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics. pp. 129-161.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the source behind the catalog's Gordon pattern (antepenult; initial in 3-syllable words), and the wording matches the catalog_quote held in webcat for kela1255 verbatim. It adds the exceptions listed above; it also records that no tone was found and that stress is not phonemic. It describes the Apoze dialect only (about 200 speakers, one of six village dialects).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Apoze dialect: stress is predictable (non-phonemic); words of one to three syllables are stressed on the first syllable, words of four or more on the antepenult, i.e. antepenultimate stress with the initial syllable stressed when the word is too short. Prefixed forms keep the stress of the stem (/aŋazi/ [aŋ'azi] 'his father' beside /azi/ ['azi]). No tone was recorded and no length contrast.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned (the intonation examples on p. 150 mark one stress per word in phrases, e.g. ma 'litamaŋotimi 'mone? 'Where is number six?', but no secondary stress is described)
new_statements.exceptions: (a) the minimal pair /awe/ [a'we] 'yesterday' vs /awe/ ['awe] 'lizard'; (b) words with a 'qualifying affix' keep the stress of the main word, so a prefixed word can be stressed on its second syllable; (c) among the paper's own transcriptions on p. 149, [taluŋa'tumi] 'rain cloud' (5 syllables) carries penultimate rather than antepenultimate stress, which the rule does not cover (possibly a compound; the paper does not comment). Three-syllable examples such as ['polowa] 'hole', ['talami] 'man', ['nambin] 'short' follow the rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are dialect-specific. Collier & Collier 1975 describe the Apoze dialect (village Lokanu', about 200 speakers; 'a little further removed from the Kela norm than any of the other villages', p. 129); the catalog record (Gordon; WALS 'Kela (Apoze)') is this variety. Johnson 1994 describes the Kuwi dialect (the task list calls it Kui; the village list on the sheet includes Kui). The OPD sheets state that each of the six Kela villages (Keila, Lagui/Lagwi, Laukanu/Lokanu, Lababia, Buso, Kui) is a different dialect.

readall_conflicts: The two opened works place stress differently and describe different dialects: Collier & Collier 1975 (Apoze dialect) give antepenultimate stress (initial in words of one to three syllables, with an affix exception and one lexical exception), whereas Johnson 1994 (Kuwi/Kui dialect) states that stress is predictable and penultimate. A third, unlisted SIL sheet obtained alongside them ('Kela [Apoze dialect] Organised Phonology Data', n.d., citing Collier 1975) repeats the Apoze antepenult statement almost word for word, so it is not independent evidence. Collier's own transcription [taluŋa'tumi] 'rain cloud' (p. 149) is penultimate in a five-syllable word, a small internal inconsistency with their rule. The catalog's antepenult coding is therefore confirmed for Apoze but not for the language as a whole

audit.recode_to: Drop 'fixed-strict antepenult' (counts as exceptionless (the strict set), antepenultimate stress). reclassify as non-strict/variable right-edge stress: penult default (obligatory in disyllables), antepenult in a lexically specified subset of 3+-syllable words, with inter-speaker and phrasal variation (Ransdell-Green 2022 sec. 2.5 pp.36-38, sec. 3.4 pp.64-66, sec. 4.5 pp.109-110, Southern Kala); keep Collier & Collier 1975 pp.149-150 as the Apoze-dialect statement (initial in 1-3 sigma, antepenult in 4+ sigma) in a dialect/caution note. Deciding source should become Ransdell-Green 2022; strength of the evidence rises (dissertation with duration measurement) while 'strict' and 'dom' flags fall.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Collier 1975 passage is present verbatim in the held scanned at printed pp.149-150 (PDF pp.21-22), sec. 3.3.1. (2) Deciding source is a 1975 SIL 'tentative phonemic statement' of one northern dialect; the best available description is Ransdell-Green's 2022 UH Manoa phonology dissertation (Glottolog's top-ranked ref, 245 pp), which we already hold but which the stress record ignores. Read at sec. 2.5/3.4/4.5 it describes penult-tending stress, always penult in disyllables, antepenult 'in some cases' for 3+-syllable words (lexical: /ˈguɾuwa/ vs /guɾuˈwaɾa/, /gaˈɾawe/, /soˈɾome/~/ˈsoɾome/), plus speaker and phrasal variation -- incompatible with a strict, exceptionless antepenult rule; Collier's own 4-5-syllable transcriptions are likewise mixed. (3) Only one un-held primary item exists (Johnson 1994 Kui OPD, 4 pp); it could not be downloaded (SIL an automated-access block, IA outag
